newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Colombia sees "banana regime" status quo remaining.
newsitem.headline: Colombia sees "banana regime" status quo remaining.

text.p: Banana exporters benefiting from European Union concessions are unlikely to suffer immediately if the World Trade Organisation confirms the practise is unfair, Colombia's Foreign Trade Minister says.

"No matter what the outcome (of a WTO appeal board) we get the sense that there is a political will to keep the status quo," Carlos Ronderos Torres told Reuters on Wednesday during a visit to Brussels.
"The choice is to comply or compensate ... we see more will to compensate," he said.

The EU has for years granted preferential treatment to certain banana producers -- chiefly former colonies of European nations -- but countries such as Colombia have also benefited after negotiating trade deals with the 15-nation bloc.
However, countries such as Mexico and Ecuador -- which produce bananas on huge plantations rather than smaller family-owned plots -- successfully petitioned the WTO to rule the EU practise unfair.
The United States, which has companies heavily involved in banana plantations outside the EU preferential bloc, initiated the WTO complaint despite not being an exporter of the fruit.
A WTO board is currently considering an appeal lodged by the European Commission.

Small banana-producing nations in the Caribbean have lamented the WTO ruling and warn that tens of thousands of farmers will go out of business if the EU is forced to reform the so-called "banana regime".
But Ronderos said there was a way out of the mire.
"This might not be a moment of crisis, but a tremendous opportunity to incorporate those countries which do not benefit from the system," he said.
"There is a very clear political will to defend the old system, but if that is not possible, we must aim to keep a market with a sense of the old."
Ronderos said that after talks with members of the Commission, the EU's executive, he was convinced the current system was unlikely to be "dismantled overnight".

"This can be negotiated satisfactorily," he said. "I would see a decision towards the end of the millennium taking into account that around this time there is likely to be a new (global trade talks) round."

Asked if European consumers should be expected to stomach the EU agreeing to compensate producers for bananas not even on sale in the 15-nation bloc in order to keep a semblance of the regime, Ronderos said:
"At the moment they (consumers) are getting good quality products and there is a demand for the product. In this way they would not directly pay any more for their bananas."
Banana consumption is soaring in Europe and Colombia alone exports $400 million of the fruit to the EU.

Germany, which eats more bananas per head than any other country in the world, has with other northern European nations long sought to scrap the current system but has been persuaded from doing so by countries such as Britain, France, Portugal and Spain.
